title: 17akhf7
The Feet in Ablution: Wiping or Washing?
hook: How do the two readings of Mâide 6 open the feet in ablution to wiping and to washing?
scenes.0.text: The sixth verse of Surah Ma'idah lists which parts of the body are to be washed and which are to be anointed. First the face, then the hands up to the elbows. Then the head is smeared and finally the feet to the heels. The debate begins with that last word. The word for "your feet" has been read in the reading tradition with two different movements, and both readings are known. The rabbinic school reads this verse as referring, not to the washing of feet, but to the anointing. According to him, the verse places the foot next to the head, which is called the mast.
scenes.0.art.actors.0.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.1.text: When the word is read with the upper movement, it seems to be attached to the limbs that are being washed, namely, the face and hands. This reading is closer to washing feet. When the verse is read with a motion, it immediately links to the word "your heads". This one's closer to the feet. Both of these arrows are said to be in the famous seven continents. The Jafari school understands and applies the recitation of the esre as a mesh command to the feet. As the head is anointed, so the feet are anointed.
scenes.1.art.actors.0.label: 5y6q5g
Reciter
scenes.1.art.actors.1.label: 1feddiq
Grammarian
scenes.2.text: In the stories from the Imams of the Ahl-i Beyt, it is described in detail how to make a foot brush. The mesh is made on the foot, from the tips of the fingers to the wrists, wet hand and the foot is not washed. Sheikh Tusi's Tehzib and Kuleynî's al-Kafî are among the main sources of this view. The Caesarian school applies Maide 6 in the light of these legends. He doesn't think foot massage is a personal choice. The recitation of the verse and the information from the Prophet's Ahl al-Bayt meet at the same point.
scenes.2.art.actors.0.label: lhg99z
Imam Ali
scenes.2.art.actors.1.label: nsaem3
Student
scenes.3.text: There are also different narratives in Sunni sources. Abu Hurayrah narrates that the Prophet said, "Woe to the heels from the fire". 165). The same warning Abdullah b. And he comes from above the command. In Buhari and Muslim, the caliph Uthman's abdest recipe also tells that feet were washed. The Sunni reading is based on these legends and bases the foot washing. The Jafari school, on the other hand, reads these words as a warning to thoroughly clean the foot and continues to brush the foot according to the **Maide 6**.
scenes.3.art.actors.0.label: kjrlmg
Person performing ablution
scenes.3.art.actors.1.label: 19izoul
The Prophet
scenes.4.text: In a tradition in Ibn Masse, Rubeyyi' bint Muawiz relates that the Prophet washed his feet. Hearing this, **Ibn Abbas** says: People insist on washing, but I find only mesh in the book of Allah. The document of the Rivayet was considered weak, and the word of Ibn Abbas was rejected by Albani. But mesh vision isn't his only one. This view is also attributed to Ali, Enes, Hasan Basri, Ikrime, Sha'bi and Ebul-Ali. It is said that Taberi recognized the right to choose between mesh and washing, while Jubba'i advocated meshi.
scenes.4.art.actors.0.label: 19xa2pv
Rubayyi'
scenes.4.art.actors.1.label: 1q0thws
Ibn Abbas
scenes.5.text: Exegetical commentators consider esre to be the most appropriate reading for the flow of the verse. And Tabataba'i and Ma'ariv prefer this reading. Some Sunnite linguists explain the verb with "cerr-i-vivar", meaning that the word takes on the verb only because of its neighbor. Some commentators find this explanation weak. Because when two words have a "and" conjunction, this kind of neighborhood effect is not very well-accepted in language. Also, mesh and wash are two separate acts. If it included the washing machine, it would be enough to wash the head.
scenes.5.art.actors.0.label: li7v2o
Commentator
scenes.5.art.actors.1.label: 1feddiq
Grammarian
scenes.6.text: The subject of mesh on a shoe or a mast also varies between schools. In Sunni sources, mesh on mast is also permitted under normal circumstances. And in the case of the jizya, the mesh is made on the bare foot. Mesh on mast is only permissible in case of need or necessity. Tabatabaei, based on some reports, writes that the Prophet's previous mest was cancelled with the 6th of Maida, i.e. removed. Thus, in Kafir practice, the original is the massage done on the bare foot.

scenes.7.text: In a nutshell, the foot in the abstracts opens up to two different applications, depending on the two readings of the verse. And he will rub his feet with it, and he will consider it a sign and a tradition of the people of the House. Most Sunnis wash their feet. Both sides will bring a sign and a narrative. The difference is seen in how the text is read, how the narratives are evaluated, and how the language is interpreted. Thus, the same verse becomes two different forms of absinthe in two schools.
sunni.0.says: Abu Hurayra tells them to perform ablution fully and reports that the Prophet said, "Woe to the heels from the Fire."
sunni.1.says: The warning "Woe to the heels from the Fire" (numbers from the IslamQA report; the text could not be reached in this session).
sunni.2.says: Caliph Uthman's description of the Prophet's abduction includes the washing of the feet.
sunni.3.says: It is related that the Prophet washed his feet; Ibn Abbas says that people insist on washing, while he finds wiping in the Book of God.
sunni.3.grade: Weak; al-Albani finds Ibn Abbas's statement munkar (from a search-result summary)
sunni.4.says: The text on Quran.com says the verse requires washing the feet; it mentions the washing narrations of Ibn Abbas and Anas, and mentions Ikrima among those who say washing. The text does not touch on the difference in reading.
sunni.5.says: The view from al-Sha'bi that wiping is permissible and the saying that Gabriel brought wiping; the narration that Anas wetted his feet while wiping.
sunni.6.says: According to al-Nawawi, the scholars agree that washing is obligatory; choice is attributed to al-Tabari, wiping to al-Jubba'i; four answers to the jarr reading (adjacency, the hadiths, the distinction between leather socks and bare feet, light washing).
sunni.7.says: Reference to Razi from WikiShia footnote (c. 11, p. 306).
shia.0.says: The Shia wash the hand downward and wipe the top of the foot; it summarizes the readings and the evidence of the two views.
shia.1.says: It is referred to as the Ehl-i Beyt riddle.
shia.2.says: A compilation of the tales of the foot Messiah from the people of the House.
shia.3.says: He prefers the reading of Cer; according to the summary of the Malang magazine, the majority, along with Shirazi, reflect the view of Shi'a.
shia.5.says: The Shia view: wiping is done on the bare foot, and no wiping over leather socks except under taqiyya and necessity.
disputes.0.title: 1h5zsns
"Your feet": fatha or kasra?
disputes.0.shia: In Mâide 6, "your feet" is read with both vowelings. In the Ja'fari reading, the kasra is a command to wipe the feet; the fatha reading can also be taken to wiping by linking it to the place of the head.
disputes.0.sunni: In Mâide 6, "your feet" is read with both vowelings. In the Sunni reading, the fatha points to washing; the kasra is interpreted as washing through adjacency, the hadiths or light washing.
disputes.1.title: 1qeerqi
The grammatical interpretation of jarr al-jiwar
disputes.1.shia: The kasra reading is the subject of two grammatical explanations. In the Ja'fari grammatical choice, when a "and" intervenes, the kasra of adjacency is weak.
disputes.1.sunni: The kasra reading is the subject of two grammatical explanations. In the Sunni explanation, the kasra agrees with the neighboring "your heads"; the meaning is washing.
disputes.2.title: gnpmxe
"Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution
disputes.2.shia: The warning "Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution also appear in Sunni books. The Ja'fari reading regards these hadiths as a warning to clean the foot well; the Ahl al-Bayt narrations report wiping.
disputes.2.sunni: The warning "Woe to the heels from the Fire" and Caliph Uthman's ablution also appear in Sunni books. In this account, the hadiths show that the Prophet washed his feet, and the verse is read in line with this practice.
disputes.3.title: 24v2t2
Wiping over leather socks
disputes.3.shia: Wiping over leather socks is mentioned in both jurisprudences. In Ja'fari practice, wiping is done on the bare foot; the verse is accepted as having abrogated the earlier wiping over leather socks.
disputes.3.sunni: Wiping over leather socks is mentioned in both jurisprudences. In the Sunni schools, this wiping is regarded as a permissible sunna even in ordinary circumstances.
questions.0: Since Mâide 6 has two recitations, how are the flow of the verse and the Prophet's practice read together to link one reading to the other?
questions.1: The document of the words attributed to Ibn Abbas, "I find a mesh in the book of Allah", was found to be weak. Why do you think this word, which is weak in the document, is still mentioned in the mesh debate?
questions.2: In the explanation of jarr al-jiwar, how does the particle "and" in between affect the view that the kasra comes from adjacency?
questions.3: The Sunni reading bases the saying "Woe to the heels from the fire" on the washing of the feet, while the Jafari school reads it as a warning to thoroughly cleanse the foot. Why do you think the same word is used in two different sentences?
summary: Two cuts of Maide 6 opens the door to the grinding and washing of the feet. It's like a little bit of rubbing on your foot. Most Sunni sects consider it obligatory to wash. Some Sunni transplants also transmit mesh vision.
key: Washing the feet or wiping them?
notes.1: The word «your feet» is read with two recitations: fatha (washing) and kasra (wiping).
notes.2: The Sunni schools wash the feet.
notes.3: Ja'fari jurisprudence, following the wiping reading of the verse, wipes over the feet.
notes.4: Practice also differs on wiping over leather socks; both schools base ablution on the Qur'an.
